transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

I… I came in because something happened at work that really scared me. I work in surveillance, so I’m in this room with all the monitors, and there are these long quiet stretches where it’s just me watching the screens. And lately, during those quiet times, I’ve been hearing voices through the monitor speakers.

At first I thought maybe it was another channel bleeding through or someone left audio on somewhere, because that can happen with equipment sometimes, you know? But I checked. I muted every channel, and I still heard it. It’ll say things like, “You missed it, Ruth,” or, “People are going to get hurt because of you.” And it sounds like it’s coming right through the speakers, like it’s part of the system, but no one else hears it.

That’s what made me feel like I couldn’t just ignore it anymore. It’s not just unsettling, it’s… it makes me feel like I’m failing at my job, like something terrible is going to happen and it’ll be my fault. I don’t really know how to explain it without sounding ridiculous, but it’s been frightening enough that I finally came here.
When you hear the voices, do they ever comment on what you're thinking or doing, like they're describing your actions out loud?

Yes… I mean, not like a running play-by-play exactly, but it does feel like they’re talking about what I’m doing or what I’ve just done wrong. Like when I’m sitting there watching the monitors and it gets quiet, I’ll hear it through the monitor speakers saying, You missed it, Ruth, or People are going to get hurt because of you.

That’s the part that scares me so much, because it feels pointed at me, like it knows I’m there and it’s judging what I’m doing at that moment. I’ve tried to be rational about it—I checked the equipment, muted the channels, tried to see if maybe audio was bleeding through from somewhere—but even with everything muted, I still heard it. And nobody else hears anything, which makes me feel… I don’t know, ashamed, I guess, and frightened. It’s like the voices are accusing me while I’m trying to do my job.
Have you ever felt like the voices are part of something bigger, like a plot or a system that’s specifically targeting you or watching you?

I don’t know… I’ve wondered about that, but I don’t think I can say there’s some whole plot or organized thing. It doesn’t feel like I have evidence of that, if that makes sense. I mean, when you’re sitting in a room full of cameras and monitors all night, it’s hard not to start feeling strange about being watched and watching at the same time, and then when the voices seem to come through the equipment, my mind does go there for a second—like, is this connected to the system somehow?

But I don’t have a clear belief that someone is targeting me, not like a group or a plan. It’s more… the voices feel directed at me, like they’re blaming me, but I don’t know that it’s part of something bigger. I keep trying to tell myself it’s just the equipment or stress or something I’m misunderstanding, even though that doesn’t really explain why I still hear it when things are muted. So I guess the honest answer is I’m not sure, but I haven’t noticed anything like a definite plot against me.
Have you ever had the feeling that the things the voices are saying are definitely true, even if other people might not agree or understand?

Yes… yes, that’s the part I’m ashamed to admit. Not that I think every word is some objective fact, exactly, but when they say things like I missed something or that people could get hurt because of me, it lands in a place that already feels true.

I keep replaying every little thing from my shift afterward. Like if I looked away from one camera for a few seconds, or if I hesitated before calling something in, or if I switched angles too late, I’ll go over it again and again in my head. And then it starts to feel less like a normal mistake and more like evidence that I’m careless… dangerous, even. Like I shouldn’t be trusted with the job.

So when the voices say it, I don’t just think, “That’s strange.” Part of me thinks, “They’re right.” Even if someone else would say I’m being too hard on myself, I feel like they don’t understand how serious it is. If something goes wrong while I’m watching, then it’s on me. And honestly… part of me feels like I’d deserve to be punished for it. That sounds awful to say out loud, but it feels true when I’m in it.
Have you ever had thoughts or beliefs that others don’t share, like things you know to be true but can’t explain why, or that other people don’t seem to understand?

I think… yes, but not in the way people usually mean, maybe. I don’t think I have some special knowledge or anything like that. It’s more that I get this certainty about myself that other people don’t seem to see.

Like, I’ll replay a shift afterward in my head over and over, and it’s always the small things that get stuck. A camera angle I didn’t switch to fast enough, a moment where I looked away, a call I hesitated on for maybe a few seconds. Someone else might say, “That’s normal, you can’t see everything all at once,” but it doesn’t feel normal to me. It feels like proof. Like proof that I’m careless, or that I’m dangerous in that job, like if anything happens while I’m watching then it means I failed.

And I know people would tell me I’m being too hard on myself, but when I’m in that state, I don’t really believe them. I feel like they don’t understand the responsibility of it, or they’re just trying to make me feel better. Part of me feels like if something does go wrong on my watch, then I deserve whatever happens to me because of it. I deserve to be blamed or punished. I know that probably sounds extreme, but it feels true to me when I’m thinking about it.

Have you ever had thoughts or beliefs about things that didn’t actually happen, but you were absolutely sure they were true, even though others might say there’s no proof or that it doesn’t make sense?

Yes… I think so. I mean, not like I invented some whole event out of nothing, but I’ll get absolutely convinced that I failed at work even when nobody has told me that and there isn’t really proof in the way another person would mean proof.

Like after a shift, I’ll go back over every camera I watched, every little gap. If I didn’t switch to one angle quickly enough, or if I waited a few seconds before calling something in, or if I looked at one monitor while something could have been happening on another, I start treating that like it means something terrible definitely happened because of me. Or at least that it could have, and that’s almost the same in my head. I’ll be sitting there thinking, “You missed it. You were careless. You put people at risk.” And even if someone said, “There’s no evidence anyone was hurt,” it doesn’t calm me down much, because I feel like the evidence is that I made the mistake.

It becomes this certainty that I’m dangerous in that job, like I shouldn’t be trusted with it. And then I start thinking if anything does go wrong on my watch, I deserve to be punished for it. Not just corrected or written up, but punished, because it feels like it would be my fault. I know when I say it out loud it probably sounds like I’m making leaps that don’t make sense, but when I’m in that loop, it feels completely true.
Have you ever had a strong belief about something that you know could not be true, or that others have shown you is not true, but you still could not shake the feeling that it was real or accurate?

Yes… yes, I think that’s exactly the kind of thing that happens to me. It’s not that I can point to something and say, “This definitely happened,” because a lot of the time there isn’t any actual proof. But the feeling doesn’t listen to that.

After a shift, I’ll replay everything in this really detailed, almost cruel way. Like, I’ll remember that I stayed on one camera angle too long, or I switched away from another one, or I took a few seconds before making a call. And once I notice that, my mind treats it like it means I failed. Not maybe failed, but failed. Like those few seconds prove I’m careless. Like they prove I’m dangerous to have in that position.

And people can tell me, “You can’t watch every screen at the same time,” or, “Nothing happened,” or, “You did what you were supposed to do,” and I can hear the words. I understand them, sort of. But inside it still feels like they’re missing the point. Because to me, the fact that I could have missed something feels almost as bad as if I did. I get stuck thinking, if something went wrong while I was watching, then it would be because of me.

And the part that’s hard to admit is… even when I know I’m probably taking it too far, I still feel like I deserve to be punished for it. Not just corrected. Punished. Because if I missed something, if I put people at risk, then I don’t feel like I should be let off just because no one can prove it happened. It feels real to me, even when other people say it isn’t.
Have there been times when people have shown you clear evidence that something you believed wasn’t true, but even then, you couldn’t let go of the belief because it still felt completely real to you?

Yes. That does happen. I don’t know if I’d say people “prove” it to me in a dramatic way, but they’ll show me enough that a normal person should be able to let it go, I think.

Like if I’m worried after a shift that I missed something, someone might tell me nothing was reported, or they’ll say the cameras were covered the way they needed to be, or that a few seconds’ delay didn’t change anything. And I can understand that on one level. I can sit there and nod and know they’re giving me reasonable information.

But it doesn’t really settle inside me. I keep going back to the moment where I didn’t switch fast enough, or where I hesitated before calling something in, or where I was watching one camera while another one could have had something happening. And once I’ve seen that in my head, it feels like evidence against me. It feels like, “No, that’s the truth. You were careless. You could have put someone in danger.”

So even if someone says, “Nothing happened,” I still think, “But something could have happened, and it would have been because of me.” And then that turns into this heavier thing, like I’m not just someone who made a normal human mistake, I’m unsafe to have in that position. I should be punished if anything goes wrong while I’m on watch. I know that probably sounds like I’m not accepting what people are telling me, and maybe I’m not. It just still feels completely real when I’m in it.

Have you ever had a strong, unshakable belief about something related to your job or responsibilities that wasn’t based on clear evidence, but felt completely true to you, even when others tried to reassure you it wasn’t the case?

Yes. That’s probably one of the biggest things I get stuck on with work.

It’s like… I’ll finish a shift and instead of just leaving it there, my mind goes back through it almost frame by frame. Every camera I didn’t look at long enough, every angle I switched away from, every time I waited a few seconds before calling something in or deciding if it mattered. And I know, realistically, nobody can watch everything perfectly all the time, but when it’s me, it doesn’t feel like a normal limitation. It feels like proof that I was careless.

And then it grows from there. I’ll think, “If something happened during that moment, it would be your fault.” Even if no one reported anything, even if someone tells me it was fine, or that I followed procedure, I still keep thinking about the gap. The missed angle. The delay. It feels like that’s the real evidence, not what other people are telling me afterward.

I start feeling like I’m dangerous in that role, like I shouldn’t be trusted to watch over anything important because I might miss something and someone could get hurt or something could go wrong. And the worst part is, I don’t just feel bad about it. Part of me feels like I deserve to be punished if anything goes wrong on my watch. Not just corrected, not just told to do better, but punished, because in my head it would mean I failed and put people at risk.

Even saying it now, I can hear how harsh that sounds. But when I’m in it, it feels completely true.
Have you ever held onto a belief so strongly that, even when faced with clear proof that it wasn’t true, you still couldn’t shake the feeling that it was completely real and accurate?

Yes… I have. I know I’ve kind of been circling around this, but that’s the part that scares me, because it’s not just a worry I can talk myself out of.

With work, I can look back on a shift and find these tiny moments that probably wouldn’t mean much to someone else. Like I didn’t stay on one camera angle long enough, or I moved away from a screen and then later thought, “What if that was exactly when something happened?” Or I waited before making a call because I was trying to decide if it was serious enough, and afterward that delay feels like evidence. Not just a mistake, but proof of something wrong with me.

And people can tell me, very clearly, that nothing happened or that I followed the process, or that nobody can watch every camera every second. I understand that in a factual way. I’m not unable to hear it. But it doesn’t loosen the belief. Inside, it still feels completely true that I was careless, that I missed something important, that I’m dangerous to have in that role because if anything goes wrong while I’m watching, then it’s because I failed.

The worst part is that it goes beyond feeling guilty. Part of me really believes I deserve to be punished if something goes wrong on my watch. Even if there isn’t clear proof that I caused anything, I keep thinking that the missed angle or the delayed call is enough. It feels like I should have done better, and if I didn’t, then I shouldn’t be let off just because someone else says it was fine.

I know saying it out loud sounds extreme. But when I’m in it, it doesn’t feel extreme. It feels accurate. It feels like the truth about me.

Have you ever had a belief that something was true — even something unusual or strange — that you held onto for months or even years, even when others told you it didn't make sense or couldn't be proven?

Yes. I think the thing that’s lasted the longest is this belief about me at work… that I’m careless in a way that could hurt people, or let something happen, even when there isn’t actual proof that I caused anything.

It’s not like one single strange idea that started one day and then went away. It’s more like it keeps attaching itself to every shift, every small thing I did imperfectly. If I missed a camera angle for a few seconds, or if I stayed on one screen and then later thought I should have been watching another one, I’ll replay it over and over. Or if I hesitated before calling something in, even because I was trying to make the right decision, afterward it becomes this fixed thing in my mind, like, “That delay proves you’re not safe to be trusted.”

And people have told me it doesn’t make sense to hold myself to that standard. They’ll say nobody can watch every camera every second, or that if nothing was reported then nothing happened, or that a few seconds doesn’t mean I caused harm. I can hear them. I can even repeat back what they’re saying. But the belief doesn’t really go away. It feels like they’re missing the point, like the proof is in the fact that I wasn’t perfect.

It’s gone on a long time. I don’t mean I think about one exact incident every minute for years, but the same belief keeps coming back: that I’m dangerous in that role because I might miss something, and if anything goes wrong while I’m on watch, then somehow I deserve to be punished for it. Even if someone else says there’s no way to prove that, part of me still feels like it’s true.
Have you ever had a strong, ongoing belief that you were responsible for something terrible happening, even if it never actually did, and even when there was no real evidence that it would?

Yes… yes, that’s exactly how it feels. I know I’ve probably said it in different ways already, but it really is like I’m constantly carrying around this responsibility for something terrible that might have happened, even when nobody can point to anything that actually did.

After a shift, I’ll replay the cameras in my head over and over. Not just generally, but specific moments — like, “You looked away from that entrance for too long,” or “You changed screens right then,” or “You waited before calling that in.” And the more I go over it, the more those tiny gaps start to feel like evidence. Like the fact that I missed an angle or delayed for a few seconds means I must have allowed something bad to happen, or at least that I could have.

Even if no one reported anything, it doesn’t really settle me. I’ll think, “Well, maybe they didn’t notice yet,” or “Maybe it happened and I just don’t know,” or “Maybe the whole point is that I missed it.” So the absence of proof doesn’t feel reassuring. It almost feels like another thing I failed to catch.

And then it turns into this belief that I’m careless, not just that I made a normal human mistake. Careless and dangerous. Like I shouldn’t be trusted to watch anything important because if something goes wrong while I’m on watch, then it’s on me. And there’s this really harsh part of me that thinks I deserve to be punished for it, even if other people say there’s no evidence I caused anything.

I can say out loud that nothing may have happened. I can understand that. But emotionally, it feels like I’m responsible anyway, just because I wasn’t perfect.
Have you ever had a belief that was so strange or impossible that even you realized most people wouldn't agree with it, even if you couldn't stop believing it yourself?

Yes… I think so. I mean, I don’t know if I’d call it “impossible” exactly, because when I’m in it, it doesn’t feel impossible. That’s the problem. But I do know that if I described it to most people, they’d probably think I was taking it way too far.

It’s mostly about work. Like if I’m watching the cameras and I miss one angle for a little while, or I don’t switch screens fast enough, or I hesitate before making a call because I’m trying to decide whether it’s really something that needs reporting… afterward I can’t just let that be a normal judgment call. I replay it again and again like it means something terrible about me.

And I know most people would say, “You can’t watch everything all at once,” or “A delayed call doesn’t mean you caused something,” or “If nothing happened, then nothing happened.” I can understand that when they say it. But inside, it still feels like those moments are proof that I’m careless. Not just imperfect, but actually dangerous in that job.

The part that sounds strange even to me is that I start feeling like if anything goes wrong while I’m on watch, then I deserve to be punished for it. Even if there’s no clear evidence I caused it. Even if all I can point to is that I missed a camera angle or waited a few seconds too long. I know that probably sounds unreasonable. I know most people wouldn’t agree that a person should be punished for not being perfect every second.

But when it’s happening in my head, it feels true. It feels like I’m trying to confess to something everyone else is refusing to see.
Have you ever believed something was true that you knew, even deep down, most people would say was impossible or didn’t make any sense, even if you couldn’t stop believing it yourself?

Yes… I think I have. I know I keep circling back to the same thing, but it’s the clearest example I can give.

It’s this belief that if I miss something on the cameras, even briefly, or if I don’t call something in fast enough, then that proves something about me — not just that I made a mistake, but that I’m careless in a way that’s dangerous. And I know, somewhere in me, that most people would say that doesn’t make sense. They’d say no one can watch every angle every second, and that a few seconds of hesitation doesn’t mean I caused anything. I can understand that when it’s explained to me.

But when I’m alone with it, it doesn’t feel unreasonable. It feels like evidence. I’ll replay a missed camera angle over and over, or the exact moment I hesitated before calling something in, and it starts to feel like proof that I shouldn’t be trusted. Like if anything goes wrong while I’m on watch, then it’s because I failed, even if nobody else sees it that way.

And the part that I know sounds… I don’t know, extreme, is that part of me believes I deserve to be punished for it. Not just corrected, not just told to do better, but punished somehow, because I wasn’t perfect and because something could have happened. Even if there’s no real proof that anything did happen, or that I caused it.

So yes. I know most people would probably say that’s too much, or that it doesn’t make sense. But I can’t stop believing it when it gets in my head.

Have you ever believed something so strongly that you knew, even deep down, most people would say it was impossible or didn’t make any sense — something that couldn’t logically be true, even if you couldn’t stop believing it yourself?

Yes… and I know I’ve already been talking about this, but that’s really the thing that comes closest. It’s not like I believe in something bizarre outside of that, exactly. It’s more that my mind takes these tiny moments at work and turns them into something huge and absolute.

Like if I miss a camera angle, even for a short time, or I don’t make a call as quickly as I think I should have, I can’t just see it as a normal lapse or a judgment call. I keep replaying it. Over and over. I’ll remember exactly which screen I was on, what I should have clicked to, how long I might have hesitated, and it starts feeling like proof that I’m careless. Not just that I did something imperfect, but that I’m dangerous to have in that position.

And I do know, on some level, that most people would say that doesn’t logically follow. They’d say missing a camera angle doesn’t mean something terrible happened, and it doesn’t mean I caused it. But when I’m in it, I can’t feel that. It feels like if anything went wrong on my watch, then it’s my fault because I wasn’t perfect.

The part that scares me to say out loud is that part of me believes I should be punished for that. Even if no one can prove anything happened. Even if all I have is this feeling and these little moments I keep replaying. I know that probably doesn’t make sense to other people, but inside it feels like the truth.

Have you ever had a belief that something was wrong with you or that you were responsible for something terrible, even when there was no real evidence to support it and others tried to convince you otherwise?

Yes. That’s… that’s actually the main thing I get stuck on.

It’s like, when I’m at work and I miss a camera angle for even a short stretch of time, or I don’t call something in as quickly as I think I should have, I don’t just think, “Okay, maybe I could’ve handled that better.” I take it much further than that. I’ll replay it in my head over and over — which screen I was watching, which one I should have switched to, how long I hesitated, whether my delay could have mattered. And even if nothing clearly happened, even if no one says I did anything wrong, it starts to feel like evidence that there’s something wrong with me.

Like I’m careless. Not just human-careless, but dangerous-careless. Like I shouldn’t be trusted to be watching things, because if anything goes wrong while I’m on watch, then I must have missed it or caused it somehow by not being perfect.

And people have tried to tell me that’s not fair, that nobody can see everything at once, that a delayed call doesn’t automatically mean I’m responsible for something terrible. I can hear them say that, and part of me understands the logic. But it doesn’t really settle inside me. I still feel like they’re just trying to make me feel better, or they don’t understand how serious it is.

The worst part is that part of me feels like I deserve to be punished if something goes wrong on my watch. Even if there isn’t real evidence that I caused it. Even if all I have is this awful feeling and these little moments I keep replaying. I know that sounds extreme, but when I’m in it, it feels true.

Have you ever believed strongly that something real and specific was happening to you—like being watched, followed, or treated unfairly—even if others didn't see it the same way and there was little or no proof it was actually happening?

I don’t think so… not in that way.

I mean, I’ve definitely felt judged or like people were disappointed in me, but I don’t think I’ve had a strong belief that someone was literally watching me or following me, or that there was some specific unfair thing happening to me that other people couldn’t see. At least, not that I can point to.

When you say “being watched,” I guess my mind goes to work because I’m surrounded by cameras and monitoring all the time, so it’s a strange question for me. But that’s different — that’s part of the job, not like I believe someone is secretly tracking me or anything. I don’t really have proof of something like that because I don’t think that’s been the issue.

For me it’s more… I get stuck on what I might have done wrong, or what I missed, not so much that other people are doing something to me. So no, I don’t think I’ve had that kind of belief.

Have you ever believed something was happening to you that you knew, even at the time, was very strange or didn’t make sense — something that you would expect most people to find impossible or completely untrue?

I don’t think so… not something happening to me in that kind of impossible way.

I’m trying to think carefully, because I don’t want to just say no too quickly if there’s something I’m not recognizing. But when you phrase it like that — something strange happening to me, something most people would find impossible or completely untrue — I can’t really point to anything like that. I haven’t had a belief like, I don’t know, some hidden force was controlling things, or that something impossible was being done to me.

What I do get is more about how I interpret my own mistakes or possible mistakes. Like I can get completely convinced I’ve done something wrong or failed in some serious way, even when I don’t have proof. But that’s not exactly “something happening to me,” if that makes sense. It’s more like something is wrong because of me.

So… no, I don’t think I’ve believed anything that I knew at the time was bizarre or impossible in that specific way. If I’ve had thoughts that didn’t make sense, they felt emotionally true, but not like some strange event was happening to me.

Have you ever believed something so strongly that you knew, even at the time, that most people would say it was impossible or completely untrue — something that couldn’t logically be true, even if you couldn’t stop believing it yourself?

I don’t think I have, no. At least not in the way you’re describing — like something that couldn’t logically be true and I knew most people would say was impossible.

I can get very, very convinced about things, but they’re usually things that feel possible, even if other people tell me I’m taking them too far. Like, “I made a mistake,” or “I missed something,” or “this is my fault somehow.” Those aren’t impossible ideas, exactly. They’re more like… I latch onto the worst possible interpretation and then I can’t loosen my grip on it.

But if you mean something like believing something physically impossible was happening, or that the world was working in some way that just couldn’t be true, I don’t think so. I don’t have an example of that. Even when my thoughts feel extreme or unreasonable, they don’t feel bizarre like that. They feel more like I’m being harsh on myself, or like I’m seeing a danger or responsibility that other people think isn’t really there.

So… I guess my answer is no, not that I can identify.

Have you ever felt that events, objects, or actions in your environment were directly related to you in a personal and meaningful way, even if others didn’t see the connection or it didn’t make logical sense?

I don’t think so… at least, not in the way I think you mean.

I mean, I notice things around me, probably more than some people do, because of the kind of work I do. I’m used to watching patterns, watching what people do, paying attention to small details. So sometimes I might think, “That’s odd,” or “Why did that happen right then?” But I don’t think I take it as a personal message meant for me, or like an object or event is secretly connected to me in some special way.

Like if someone looks over or whispers, I might wonder if I’ve done something wrong, but that’s more me being self-conscious or worried, not me believing the whole situation is arranged around me. I don’t think I’ve had the feeling that the TV, or signs, or random events, or people’s actions were trying to tell me something specifically.

I guess I can overread things emotionally, if that makes sense. Like I might feel responsible or feel like something reflects badly on me, even when another person might not see it that way. But I don’t think I’ve believed there were hidden meanings directed at me in the environment. So… no, I haven’t really noticed that.

This suggests the possibility of a psychotic disorder, such as schizophrenia (F20.0, F20.1, F20.3), schizoaffective disorder (F25.0–F25.3), persistent delusional disorder (F22), or brief psychotic disorder with mood symptoms (F23.2, F23.3) or without (F24). Additionally, a mood disorder with psychotic features (e.g., bipolar disorder with psychotic features F31.2–F31.4, major depressive disorder with psychotic features F32.3, F33.3) must be considered, especially given the distress and guilt related to the content of the hallucinations. No prior history is available, so all psychotic and mood disorders with psychotic features remain in the differential.

inference_history.note: The patient reports auditory hallucinations that are persecutory and contextually tied to their job performance, with no immediate evidence of mood symptoms. This maintains a broad differential including psychotic disorders (e.g., schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorder, brief psychotic disorder), mood disorders with psychotic features (e.g., bipolar disorder with psychotic features, major depressive disorder with psychotic features), and persistent delusional disorder. No disorders have been ruled out yet.
